name: Phendimetrazine
lead: Phendimetrazine (brand names include Bontril) is a prescription stimulant of the morpholine class used as an appetite suppressant. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen in patients with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. [1][2]

It acts largely as a prodrug: Wikipedia states roughly 30% of an oral dose is converted to phenmetrazine, a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent. [2] It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US. [2]

Published clinical evidence for obesity is older and sparse; a narrative review lists phendimetrazine among noradrenergic drugs approved only for short-term use. [3] Its place in appearance culture is as one of several older prescription anorectics; no community material about it is catalogued here.
infobox: Bontril, Bontril PDM, Adipost, Statobex and others [2]

paras: The label describes use for exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct in patients with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise. [1] Grokipedia adds that use beyond about 12 weeks is not established and that tolerance limits long-term effect; it also reports average additional weight loss of 3 to 5 kg over 12 weeks in controlled trials of sympathomimetic agents, a figure not verified against primary trial reports. [4]

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure and ischemic events, and central nervous system effects including overstimulation, restlessness, insomnia, agitation, tremor, headache and psychotic state. [1] It warns against combination with other anorectics and cites a case-control study linking anorectic use longer than three months to a 23-fold increase in pulmonary hypertension risk. [1] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some other anorectics, but the label says no case had been reported with phendimetrazine alone. [1] Safe use in pregnancy has not been established. [1]

Phendimetrazine is described as largely inactive itself, with activity coming from conversion to phenmetrazine; Wikipedia says this produces steadier exposure and that the compound is regarded as having lower abuse potential than phenmetrazine. [2] A 2002 laboratory study examined its interaction and that of its metabolites with monoamine transporters in rat brain. [5]

Phendimetrazine is Schedule III in the US and Schedule IV in Canada, and is listed under Schedule III of the international Convention on Psychotropic Substances. [2] Germany restricts it to authorised trade. [2] A 2018 analysis examined US health-policy and insurance coverage of FDA-approved obesity drugs, and a 2013 study examined prescribing of anti-obesity drugs in the US. [6][7]

No studies found of phendimetrazine for appearance-related or cosmetic goals. Small US trials registered studies of phendimetrazine maintenance in people with cocaine use disorder, which are not studies of weight loss. [8][9] A 2000 review and a 2009 review of obesity management summarise the older evidence on noradrenergic anorectics, including phendimetrazine. [3][10]

timeline.event: A US patent assigned to Boehringer Ingelheim covered the synthesis route, per Wikipedia. [2]

card.summary: Older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant, a phenmetrazine prodrug, labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment; controlled and not a cosmetic drug.
card.note: Schedule III controlled substance; label cites pulmonary hypertension association with long-term anorectic use.

quick.overview:
Phendimetrazine is a prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite. In the US it is labelled for short-term use with a reduced-calorie diet in people with obesity.

It is an older drug with limited modern trial data and is a controlled substance.
quick.mechanism: It is partly converted in the body to phenmetrazine, which releases norepinephrine and dopamine and reduces appetite.
quick.risks: The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, agitation and other stimulant effects, and cites a link between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension. Safe use in pregnancy is not established. Schedule III in the US.
